title: Computer Fundamentals
subtitle: Hardware vs software, memory units (bit/byte/KB/MB/GB), I/O devices, OS basics, and the five generations of computers

readingSections.title: Hardware vs Software: What a Computer Actually Is
readingSections.quickSummary: Hardware is the physical machine you can touch; software is the set of instructions that tells the hardware what to do. Neither works without the other.
content: A computer is a programmable machine that takes input, processes it, and produces output. It has two halves: HARDWARE (the physical parts - chips, wires, screen, keyboard, the box itself) and SOFTWARE (the programs - the operating system, the browser, Word, the calculator). Think of hardware as the kitchen and software as the recipe: you need both to cook anything.

HARDWARE examples: CPU (the brain), RAM (short-term memory), hard disk / SSD (long-term memory), motherboard, monitor, keyboard, mouse, printer, USB drive, graphics card. If you can pick it up and drop it, it is hardware.

SOFTWARE comes in two flavours. SYSTEM SOFTWARE is the operating system (Windows, macOS, Linux, Android) plus low-level utilities - it runs the machine. APPLICATION SOFTWARE is what you actually open to do work: Chrome, Excel, WhatsApp, a music player. System software sits underneath; application software sits on top.

Programming languages (Python, Java, C, JavaScript) are not software by themselves - they are the tools you use to WRITE software. The final .exe or .app or .apk file the user double-clicks is the software.

Why placement tests ask this: every Accenture AXIS 'Common Applications & MS Office' MCQ block assumes you know the difference. 'Is MS Word hardware or software?' is a 30-second question that should be free.

subsections.title: The simple test that always works
subsections.content: If you can physically damage it by dropping it -> hardware. If you can copy it to a USB drive -> software. A virus is software. A broken screen is a hardware problem. A frozen screen can be EITHER (software bug or hardware fault).

subsections.title: Firmware: the in-between
subsections.content: Firmware is software that lives permanently inside a hardware device - the program inside your router, washing machine, or the BIOS/UEFI chip on your motherboard. You rarely touch it, but it is software stored in hardware.

quickRevision: Hardware = physical; Software = instructions.
System software = OS + utilities; Application software = Word, Chrome, games.
Programming language != software; software is the program the language produces.
Firmware = software stored permanently in a hardware device.
tricks: If the option says 'set of instructions' -> software.
If the option says 'physical component' / 'tangible' / 'electronic' -> hardware.
Virus / malware / app = software. Monitor / CPU / printer = hardware.
patterns: 'A program is a set of...' -> instructions (software).
'Which is NOT hardware?' with a list of devices + 1 program -> pick the program.
'Which is application software?' -> MS Word, Excel, Photoshop (not Windows, not Linux).

pyqPatterns.question: Which of the following is hardware?
pyqPatterns.approach: Pick the physical device (CPU / Monitor / Keyboard), reject OS / program / data.

pyqPatterns.question: MS Word is an example of:
pyqPatterns.approach: Application software - it is a program the user runs to do work.

readingSections.title: Memory Units: Bits, Bytes, KB, MB, GB, TB
readingSections.quickSummary: A bit is 0 or 1. A nibble is 4 bits. A byte is 8 bits and stores one character. Every step up is roughly 1000x bigger (technically 1024x in binary).
content: A computer only understands two things: 0 and 1. A single 0-or-1 value is called a BIT (short for binary digit). It is the smallest possible piece of data.

8 bits together = 1 BYTE. A byte is the basic unit computers use to store a single character like 'A', '7', or '?'. Because 8 bits can combine in 256 ways (2 to the power 8), a byte can represent any of 256 different symbols - which is why early alphabets like ASCII had exactly 256 characters.
4 bits = 1 NIBBLE (also called a 'half byte' or 'nybble'). A nibble holds one hexadecimal digit (0-9, A-F). You will see nibbles in hex colour codes (#FF5733) and in BCD (Binary Coded Decimal) work.

Above the byte, units climb by 1024 each step (in the binary convention) or by 1000 each step (in the decimal convention). Most placement exams use 1024. So 1 KB = 1024 bytes, 1 MB = 1024 KB, 1 GB = 1024 MB, 1 TB = 1024 GB. The exact byte counts are powers of 2: 1 KB = 2^10 bytes, 1 MB = 2^20 bytes, 1 GB = 2^30 bytes, 1 TB = 2^40 bytes.

Roughly: a 3-page text file is a few KB; an MP3 song is 3-5 MB; a DVD holds 4.7 GB; a typical laptop SSD is 512 GB to 2 TB; cloud data centres store petabytes (PB) and beyond. Knowing the order of magnitude is what exam options test.

subsections.title: The exact byte counts you must memorise
subsections.content:
1 byte = 8 bits
1 KB = 1,024 bytes = 2^10
1 MB = 1,024 KB = 1,048,576 bytes = 2^20
1 GB = 1,024 MB = 1,073,741,824 bytes = 2^30
1 TB = 1,024 GB = 1,099,511,627,776 bytes = 2^40
1 PB = 1,024 TB = 2^50 bytes
The trick: when an option shows 1,000, 1,000,000 or 1,000,000,000 it is the DECIMAL convention (used by hard drive marketing). The placement-exam answer is 1,024, 1,048,576, 1,073,741,824.

subsections.title: Why 1024 and not 1000
subsections.content: Computers think in binary. 1000 in decimal is not a round number in binary (it is 1111101000). 1024 is 2^10, which is binary-round. So memory addresses step in 1024-byte blocks. Disk-drive manufacturers cheat and use 1000 (decimal) so a '1 TB' drive shows as ~931 GB in Windows.

subsections.title: Word size in modern CPUs
subsections.content: A WORD is the natural data size a CPU handles in one instruction. Older CPUs were 8-bit or 16-bit; modern laptops/desktops are 64-bit. So a 64-bit machine can fetch 8 bytes at a time. Exams sometimes ask this - answer is 64 bits on a modern PC.

quickRevision: 1 bit = 0 or 1 (smallest).
1 nibble = 4 bits (one hex digit).
1 byte = 8 bits = 1 character.
1 KB = 1024 bytes; 1 MB = 1024 KB; 1 GB = 1024 MB; 1 TB = 1024 GB.
Each step is also 2^10, 2^20, 2^30, 2^40 in bytes.
Modern CPU word = 64 bits.
tricks: If the option says 1000, 1000000, 1000000000 -> decimal convention, not the placement exam answer.
If the question asks 'smallest unit' -> bit, not byte or nibble.
If the question asks 'next bigger than byte' -> kilobyte (KB), NOT megabyte.
TB -> PB -> EB -> ZB -> YB ladder. 1 PB > 1 TB (trap: 'petabyte is smaller than terabyte' is wrong).
patterns: '1 character is stored in?' -> 1 byte (for ASCII).

readingSections.title: Input and Output Devices
readingSections.quickSummary: Input devices send data TO the computer (keyboard, mouse, scanner, mic). Output devices send data FROM the computer (monitor, printer, speaker). Some are both (touchscreen, modem, hard disk).
content: An INPUT DEVICE converts what a human does (typing, clicking, speaking, scanning) into data the computer can process. Common input devices: keyboard, mouse (the default pointing device on a desktop), touchpad/trackpad, scanner, microphone, joystick, digital camera, barcode reader, light pen, graphics tablet, fingerprint scanner.

An OUTPUT DEVICE takes processed data and presents it to a human. Common output devices: monitor (also called VDU - Visual Display Unit), printer, speakers, headphones, plotter (for large engineering drawings), projector.

Some devices work BOTH ways and are called INPUT/OUTPUT devices. The classic example is the TOUCHSCREEN - you tap it (input) and it shows you a result (output). Modems, network interface cards (NIC), and hard disks (they READ data and WRITE data) also fall here. Touchscreen and modem are the two the exam loves to test.

Two scanner-family devices that confuse students: OCR (Optical Character Recognition) scans PRINTED text and turns it into editable text. MICR (Magnetic Ink Character Recognition) reads the magnetic ink on the bottom of cheques - that is why the cheque number at the bottom of a bank cheque uses a special font. Barcode readers read product barcodes in shops.

Printers come in three flavours for exams: IMPACT (dot matrix - strikes the paper, noisy, used for carbon copies); NON-IMPACT (inkjet - sprays ink; laser - uses toner and a heated roller, fastest and most common). Plotter prints vector graphics on large paper (engineering / architecture drawings).

subsections.title: Pointing devices
subsections.content: The mouse is the default pointing device on a desktop computer (Scientech Easy: 'mouse is the most common pointing device'). A trackball is a mouse turned upside-down - you spin the ball with your fingers instead of moving the whole mouse (good for limited-desk setups). A touchpad is a flat surface you slide your finger across (laptops). A joystick is a stick for games / flight sims.

subsections.title: Storage vs I/O - the overlap
subsections.content: Hard disks, SSDs, USB drives, optical drives (CD/DVD/Blu-ray) are STORAGE devices, but they are also I/O devices because the computer reads from them (input) and writes to them (output). Exams usually call them 'secondary storage' or 'auxiliary storage' rather than I/O. Do not be tricked by an option that says 'hard disk is an output device' - it can act as one but the textbook category is storage.

subsections.title: VDU vs Monitor
subsections.content: VDU = Visual Display Unit. It is the same thing as a monitor. Old exam papers use VDU; new ones use monitor. Both answers are correct if both are in the options.

quickRevision: Input: keyboard, mouse, scanner, mic, joystick, touchpad, OCR, MICR, barcode reader.
Output: monitor/VDU, printer (inkjet/laser/dot matrix), speaker, plotter, projector.
Both: touchscreen, modem, hard disk (storage + I/O).
Mouse = default pointing device on a desktop.
OCR scans printed text; MICR reads cheque ink.
tricks: If the stem says 'reads cheques' -> MICR. If 'scans printed text' -> OCR / scanner.
If asked 'which is NOT an input device' and the options include monitor -> monitor is output, so it is the answer.
Touchscreen and modem are the exam's favourite 'both' traps - they test whether you know I/O vs storage categories.
patterns: 'Which device scans printed text?' -> Scanner / OCR.
'Which is used to read barcodes in shops?' -> Barcode reader.
'Which is an output device?' -> Monitor, printer, speaker (NOT keyboard, NOT scanner).
'Which is a pointing device?' -> Mouse, trackball, touchpad, joystick, light pen.

readingSections.title: Operating System Basics
readingSections.quickSummary: An operating system (OS) is the master program that manages the hardware and lets applications run. It handles memory, processes, files, devices, and security. Examples: Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS.
content: An OPERATING SYSTEM (OS) is the system software that controls the entire computer. Without an OS, an application cannot run. When you turn on a computer, the OS loads first; then everything else (browser, editor, games) runs ON TOP of the OS. Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS, and Unix are all operating systems.

The OS does five big jobs. (1) PROCESS MANAGEMENT - decides which running program (process) gets the CPU right now, and switches between them thousands of times per second. (2) MEMORY MANAGEMENT - tracks which parts of RAM each process is using and stops them from stomping on each other. (3) FILE MANAGEMENT - organises files and folders on disk and handles reads/writes. (4) DEVICE MANAGEMENT - talks to printers, keyboards, disks, network cards via drivers. (5) SECURITY / ACCESS CONTROL - decides who can open which file or use which program.

The KERNEL is the core part of the OS that runs in privileged 'kernel mode' with direct access to hardware. The rest of the OS - the shell, the desktop, the file explorer - runs in 'user mode' and asks the kernel to do the dangerous bits. This split is called DUAL-MODE OPERATION and is what stops a buggy app from crashing the whole machine.

Three key OS concepts the exam tests. MULTIPROGRAMMING keeps several programs in memory at once so the CPU is never idle. MULTITASKING is the user-visible version - running multiple apps at once and switching between them (Alt-Tab). TIME-SHARING is a flavour of multitasking where the CPU time is divided into small slices and given to each user in turn - it is what made mainframes serve many users at once in the 1960s-70s.

subsections.title: Spooling
subsections.content: SPOOL = Simultaneous Peripheral Operations Online. The OS pretends to print immediately by saving the print job to a queue on disk; the printer prints from the queue at its own speed while you keep working. The exam definition is verbatim: 'a process of temporarily storing data in a buffer so it can be processed by a device at its own pace'.

subsections.title: OS examples you should be able to name
subsections.content: Desktop: Windows (Microsoft, dominant), macOS (Apple), Linux (open source, Ubuntu/Fedora/Debian flavours). Mobile: Android (Google, Linux kernel), iOS (Apple). Servers / mainframes: Linux, Unix (Solaris, AIX). Note: Android is technically a Linux distribution; the exam sometimes asks if Android is an OS (yes) and what kernel it uses (Linux).

subsections.title: Functions the exam asks about directly
subsections.content: Memory management, file management, process management, device management, security. The classic PYQ stem is: 'Which of the following is NOT a function of an OS?' with options that mix in 'web browsing' or 'compiling code' - those are application functions, not OS functions.

quickRevision: OS = system software that manages hardware and runs applications.
5 jobs: process, memory, file, device, security management.
Kernel = core, runs in privileged mode; user programs run in user mode.
Multiprogramming = many programs in memory. Multitasking = user sees many at once. Time-sharing = many users, slices of CPU.
Examples: Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS, Unix.
Spooling = queue print jobs on disk so the printer works at its own pace.
tricks: If the stem says 'NOT a function of OS' and an option is 'compiling' / 'web browsing' / 'word processing' -> that is the answer (it is an application function).
Android is a Linux-based OS (not a separate kernel).
Kernel is part of the OS, not a separate program. Driver is part of OS support, not the OS itself.
patterns: 'Which is NOT a function of the OS?' -> pick the user / application task.
'The core of the OS is called:' -> kernel.
'The OS manages...' -> processes, memory, files, devices, security.

pyqPatterns.approach: Pick the user task (e.g. 'editing a document'); the OS does not edit - the application does.

readingSections.title: The Five Generations of Computers
readingSections.quickSummary: 1st = vacuum tubes (1940s-50s). 2nd = transistors (50s-60s). 3rd = integrated circuits (60s-70s). 4th = microprocessors (70s-present). 5th = AI + ULSI (present-future).
content: The story of computers is usually told in FIVE GENERATIONS, each defined by the core electronic component. Every generation got smaller, faster, cheaper, and more reliable than the one before. The exam almost always asks one of three things: which generation used which component, which language was used, or which computer was an example.

FIRST GENERATION (1940s-1950s) used VACUUM TUBES. A vacuum tube is a sealed glass tube that controls electron flow - it is big, hot, fragile, and burns out often. ENIAC (Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer) used about 18,000 vacuum tubes. EDVAC and UNIVAC were other 1st-gen machines. Programs were in MACHINE LANGUAGE (raw 0s and 1s). Memory was magnetic drums and magnetic tape. Input was paper tape and punched cards. They filled entire rooms, generated huge heat, and needed constant maintenance.

SECOND GENERATION (1950s-1960s) replaced vacuum tubes with TRANSISTORS. A transistor is a tiny semiconductor device that does the same switching job but with much less heat, less power, and far higher reliability. Memory moved to magnetic cores and magnetic tape / disk. Programming shifted to ASSEMBLY and early HIGH-LEVEL languages: FORTRAN (1956), ALGOL (1958), COBOL (1959). Example machines: PDP-8, IBM 1400 series, IBM 7090/7094, UNIVAC 1107, CDC 3600.

THIRD GENERATION (1960s-1970s) used INTEGRATED CIRCUITS (ICs) - many transistors packed onto a single silicon chip. The OS arrived in this era, which let computers run multiple programs at once. Programming was in true HIGH-LEVEL languages (BASIC became popular here). Memory: large magnetic core. I/O: monitor, keyboard, printer, magnetic tape. Example machines: IBM 360, IBM 370, PDP-11, NCR 395, UNIVAC 1108.

subsections.title: FOURTH GENERATION (1970s-Present)
subsections.content: The MICROPROCESSOR defines the 4th generation - the entire CPU on a single chip. The Intel 4004 (1971) is widely cited as the first commercial microprocessor. VLSI (Very Large Scale Integration) put thousands of transistors on one chip. Memory shifted to SEMICONDUCTOR memory (RAM, ROM). Operating systems added time-sharing, multiprogramming, multiprocessing and virtual memory. Personal computers appeared: IBM PC (1981), Apple II, Apple Macintosh. This is the generation we are in - the laptop, desktop, and smartphone all use 4th-gen technology.

subsections.title: FIFTH GENERATION (Present-Future)
subsections.content: The defining tech is ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE - voice recognition, natural-language understanding, machine learning, robotics. Hardware uses ULSI (Ultra Large Scale Integration) with millions of transistors per chip and parallel processing (multiple CPUs working together). The goal: computers that behave like humans. We are partway into the 5th generation; full human-level AI is still a research target. Examples: modern AI assistants, voice-controlled smartphones, self-driving cars, IBM Watson, modern GPUs running neural networks.

subsections.title: The three things every MCQ on this topic tests
subsections.content: (a) Component match: vacuum tube = 1st, transistor = 2nd, IC = 3rd, microprocessor = 4th, AI/ULSI = 5th. (b) Period range: if you remember '40s = 1st, 50s-60s = 2nd, 60s-70s = 3rd, 70s-present = 4th' you can answer any 'in which generation' stem. (c) Examples: ENIAC = 1st, PDP-8 = 2nd, IBM 360 = 3rd, IBM PC = 4th.

quickRevision: 1st: 1940s-50s, vacuum tubes, machine language, ENIAC / EDVAC / UNIVAC.
2nd: 1950s-60s, transistors, FORTRAN / COBOL, PDP-8 / IBM 1400.
3rd: 1960s-70s, integrated circuits, BASIC, IBM 360 / PDP-11.
4th: 1970s-present, microprocessors (Intel 4004 1971), VLSI, IBM PC / Apple.
5th: present-future, AI + ULSI, parallel processing, voice / NLP.
tricks: Component-to-generation is one-way; if the option lists 'microprocessors' against 1st, 2nd, 3rd -> pick 4th.
ENIAC = 1st (with ~18,000 vacuum tubes) - the exam loves this number.
If the question is about the 'first microprocessor' -> Intel 4004 (1971), 4th generation.
If the question is about 'first high-level language' in 2nd gen -> FORTRAN (1956).
Batch processing = 1st generation. Time-sharing and multiprogramming = 4th.
patterns: 'Microprocessors are the basis of which generation?' -> 4th.
'ENIAC was an example of which generation?' -> 1st.

formulas.title: Memory Unit Ladder (1024-Step Rule)

formula.text: Each step up the ladder multiplies by 1024 (or 2^10). The byte count grows by 2^10 each time.

formulas.whenToUse: Any 'how many bytes in X KB / MB / GB / TB?' question, and any 'which is larger / smaller' between two units.
explanation: 1 KB = 1,024 bytes. The decimal value 1,000 is the marketing convention; the placement exam uses 1,024.
1 MB = 1,024 KB = 1,048,576 bytes. The 1,048,576 is 2^20 - memorise this number.
1 GB = 1,024 MB = 1,073,741,824 bytes (2^30). This exact number shows up as an option.
Order from smallest to largest: Bit < Nibble < Byte < KB < MB < GB < TB < PB < EB < ZB < YB.
When the question asks for the next-bigger unit, step one ladder rung up - KB after byte, MB after KB, etc.
formulas.memoryTip: Think 'K = Kilo = thousand-ish'. Real value: 1,024. Each 'K/M/G/T' is 2^10 / 2^20 / 2^30 / 2^40 bytes.
formulas.commonMistake: Choosing 1,000 / 1,000,000 / 1,000,000,000 - those are decimal (drive marketing) and are wrong for placement exams.

formulas.title: Bit-Byte-Nibble Conversions

formula.text: Bits -> bytes: divide by 8. Bytes -> bits: multiply by 8. Nibble = 4 bits (one hex digit).

formulas.whenToUse: Conversions between bits and bytes, and any nibble / hex-digit question.
explanation: 1 byte = 8 bits. Always. 1 character (ASCII) = 1 byte = 8 bits.
1 nibble = 4 bits. Nibble = half a byte. One nibble holds one hexadecimal digit (0-F).
Bytes to bits: multiply by 8. Bits to bytes: divide by 8.
Two nibbles make one byte.
A 'word' on a 64-bit CPU = 64 bits = 8 bytes.
formulas.memoryTip: '8 bits make a byte, 4 bits make a nibble.' Nibble = half-byte, byte = full.
formulas.commonMistake: Confusing nibble (4 bits) with byte (8 bits); 4-bits and 8-bits are different sizes.

formulas.title: I/O Device Classification

formula.text: Keyboard/mouse/scanner/mic/joystick = input. Monitor/printer/speaker/plotter = output. Touchscreen/modem/hard disk = both.

formulas.whenToUse: Any 'is this device input, output, or both?' MCQ. Most common I/O block questions.
explanation: INPUT devices convert human action into data: keyboard, mouse, scanner, mic, joystick, touchpad, OCR, MICR, barcode reader, digital camera, light pen.
OUTPUT devices convert data into something a human senses: monitor / VDU, printer (inkjet / laser / dot matrix), speaker, plotter, projector.
BOTH-WAY devices: touchscreen (you tap, it shows), modem (sends and receives), network card, hard disk (reads and writes).
Mouse = default pointing device on a desktop. Trackball = mouse upside-down. Touchpad = laptop flat surface. Joystick = game / flight-sim stick.
OCR scans printed text. MICR reads magnetic-ink characters on cheques. Barcode reader scans product codes.
Hard disk is technically an I/O device but the textbook label is 'secondary storage'.

example.prompt: Which of the following is an output device?
steps: Check each option against the input / output / both lists.
Monitor -> output. Keyboard -> input. Touchscreen -> both. Mouse -> input.

formulas.memoryTip: INPUT = I (the human puts something in). OUTPUT = human looks/listens. BOTH = the device can do both (touchscreen, modem, hard disk).
formulas.commonMistake: Listing a hard disk as 'pure output' or 'pure input' - it is storage and acts as both.

formulas.title: Generation-Component-Time Matching

formula.text: Match each generation to its core hardware and period. One memory ladder: tube -> transistor -> IC -> microprocessor -> AI.

formulas.whenToUse: Any 'which generation used X?' or 'in which generation did Y appear?' MCQ.
explanation: 1st gen (1940s-50s) = vacuum tubes. ENIAC (~18,000 tubes), EDVAC, UNIVAC. Machine language. Magnetic tape / drum.
2nd gen (1950s-60s) = transistors. FORTRAN 1956, COBOL 1959. Magnetic core memory. PDP-8, IBM 1400.
3rd gen (1960s-70s) = integrated circuits. BASIC, OS appears. IBM 360, PDP-11.
4th gen (1970s-present) = microprocessors. Intel 4004 (1971). VLSI. Personal computers (IBM PC, Apple).
5th gen (present-future) = AI, ULSI, parallel processing. Voice recognition, NLP, machine learning.
Batch processing belongs to the 1st gen. Time-sharing, multiprogramming, multiprocessing -> 4th gen.

steps: 1st = vacuum tube, 2nd = transistor, 3rd = IC, 4th = microprocessor, 5th = AI/ULSI.

formulas.memoryTip: Read top to bottom: tube, transistor, IC, microprocessor, AI. The 'shrinking' story: each generation fits more into less space.
formulas.commonMistake: Picking 'transistor' for the microprocessor question. Transistor = 2nd, microprocessor = 4th. They are NOT the same.

Monitor / printer / speaker are output.

mcqs.q: The default pointing device on a desktop computer is the:
exp: Mouse is the standard desktop pointing device.

mcqs.q: Which is an output device?
exp: Monitor / VDU displays output.
Scanner, mic, joystick are input.

mcqs.q: MICR is used to read:
exp: MICR = Magnetic Ink Character Reader. Bank cheque routing numbers are printed in magnetic ink.

mcqs.q: OCR stands for:
exp: OCR = Optical Character Recognition. Scans printed text -> editable digital text.

mcqs.q: Which device is BOTH input and output?
exp: Touchscreen takes taps (input) and displays (output).
Modem and hard disk are also both-way.

mcqs.q: The core part of an operating system is the:
exp: The kernel is the OS core that talks directly to hardware.
Shell / driver / desktop are layers built on top of the kernel.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a function of an operating system?
exp: Compiling is done by a compiler (a user application).
OS handles memory, processes, files, devices, security.

mcqs.q: An operating system manages:
exp: The OS mediates between hardware and applications - managing both.

mcqs.q: Which is an example of an operating system?
exp: Linux is an OS. Windows, macOS, Android, iOS, Unix are others.
Word / Chrome / Photoshop are applications.

mcqs.q: Android is based on the:
exp: Android is a Linux-based OS. Linux kernel + Android userland.

mcqs.q: SPOOL stands for:
exp: SPOOL = Simultaneous Peripheral Operations Online. The OS queues print jobs on disk so the printer works at its own pace.

mcqs.q: First-generation computers used:
exp: 1st gen (1940s-50s) = vacuum tubes.

mcqs.q: Transistors replaced vacuum tubes in which generation?
exp: 2nd gen (1950s-60s) = transistors.

mcqs.q: Integrated circuits characterise which generation?
exp: 3rd gen (1960s-70s) = integrated circuits (ICs).

mcqs.q: Microprocessors are the basis of which generation?
exp: 4th gen (1970s-present) = microprocessors.

mcqs.q: ENIAC used approximately how many vacuum tubes?
exp: ENIAC had about 18,000 vacuum tubes - a published PYQ number.

mcqs.q: FORTRAN was developed in:
exp: FORTRAN (1956), COBOL (1959) - 2nd-generation high-level languages.

mcqs.q: The first commercial microprocessor was the:
exp: Intel 4004 (1971) is widely credited as the first commercial microprocessor - 4th gen.

mcqs.q: Which generation is associated with Artificial Intelligence?
exp: 5th gen = AI, ULSI, parallel processing, NLP, voice recognition.

mcqs.q: IBM 360 is an example of which generation?
exp: IBM 360 and PDP-11 are 3rd-gen (ICs) classics.

mcqs.q: Batch processing was characteristic of which generation?
exp: 1st-gen mainframes ran batch jobs (no interactive time-sharing yet).

mcqs.q: A word on a 64-bit CPU is:
exp: Modern desktop / laptop CPUs are 64-bit - 64 bits per word.

mcqs.q: How many distinct values can one byte represent?
exp: 2^8 = 256 distinct values (0-255).
255 is the maximum VALUE; there are 256 distinct values.

mcqs.q: How many bytes in 1 GB (binary)?
Which is the correct order from smallest to largest?
exp: 1 bit < 4-bit nibble < 8-bit byte.

mcqs.q: 1 character (ASCII) takes up:
exp: ASCII characters fit in 1 byte (7-8 bits).

mcqs.q: 32 bits is equal to:
exp: 32 / 8 = 4 bytes.

mcqs.q: A trackball is a pointing device that:
opts: You spin the ball with your fingers
exp: A trackball is a mouse turned upside-down - you spin the ball with your fingers.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT a pointing device?
exp: Plotter is an output device. Mouse / light pen / joystick are pointing devices.

mcqs.q: A plotter is most often used for:
exp: Plotters print vector graphics on large paper - engineering / architecture drawings.

mcqs.q: A laser printer uses:
exp: Laser printer = toner + heated roller. Inkjet = sprayed liquid. Dot matrix = striking pins.

mcqs.q: A dot matrix printer is an example of:
exp: Dot matrix strikes an inked ribbon against paper - impact printer.

mcqs.q: VDU stands for:
exp: VDU = Visual Display Unit. Another name for the monitor.

mcqs.q: A hard disk is best classified as:
exp: Hard disk is secondary storage (not I/O, not software).

mcqs.q: Which is NOT a function of an operating system?
exp: Web browsing is done by an application (browser).
Memory / file / process / device / security management are OS jobs.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT an operating system?
exp: MS Excel is an application. Windows / Linux / macOS are operating systems.

mcqs.q: Multitasking means:
opts: Running one program at a time
Running multiple programs and switching between them
exp: Multitasking = the user sees multiple programs running and switches between them (Alt-Tab).

mcqs.q: Time-sharing operating systems allow:
opts: One user to run one program
Many users to share a computer by taking CPU slices
exp: Time-sharing = CPU time divided into small slices, each user / program gets turns. Made mainframes serve many users.

mcqs.q: The OS is loaded into memory:
opts: Only when a file is opened
exp: The OS loads first when the computer boots. Everything else runs on top of it.

mcqs.q: Which language was developed in the 2nd generation of computers?
exp: FORTRAN 1956, COBOL 1959, ALGOL 1958 are 2nd-gen languages.
BASIC is 3rd gen. Python / Java are 4th gen.

mcqs.q: COBOL was developed in:
exp: COBOL 1959 - 2nd-generation language.

mcqs.q: Personal computers (IBM PC, Apple II) appeared in which generation?
exp: PCs arrived in the 4th gen, enabled by the microprocessor.

mcqs.q: Which generation used the VLSI (Very Large Scale Integration) technology?
exp: VLSI = 4th generation. ULSI = 5th generation.

mcqs.q: Natural language understanding is a goal of which generation?
exp: 5th gen aims: AI, natural-language understanding, parallel processing.

mcqs.q: Firmware is:
opts: Software stored permanently inside a hardware device
exp: Firmware is software that lives permanently in a hardware device (router BIOS, washing-machine controller).

mcqs.q: What is the next unit larger than a gigabyte?
exp: Order: KB -> MB -> GB -> TB -> PB.
After GB comes TB.

mcqs.q: Application software runs:
opts: On top of the operating system
Directly on the hardware without an OS
exp: Applications run ON TOP OF the OS, which mediates hardware access.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an example of an I/O device?
exp: Keyboard is an input device. Hard disk is usually classified as storage, not I/O.
MS Word and the Linux kernel are software.

mcqs.q: A scanner is an example of:
exp: Scanner reads paper into the computer - input.

mcqs.q: Memory unit order smallest to largest:
exp: Each step is ~1000x bigger: KB < MB < GB < TB.

mcqs.q: The 1st-generation computers were programmed in:
exp: 1st-gen = machine language (raw 0s and 1s). High-level languages came in the 2nd gen (FORTRAN 1956).
